---
title: "Analysing clades and traits in a metacommunity"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6)
```

This article goes through the two analyses of metacommunity phylogenetics in the package:
the node regression of Leibold et al. (2010) with their daphniids, and the phylogenetic
gradient analysis of Peres-Neto et al. (2012) with simulated data, which are the methods
checked in the article on validation.

```{r}
library(comdynamite)
```

## Which clades respond to the environment?

`daphniids` rebuilds the data of Leibold et al. (2010) from the public survey: presences of
13 species in lakes of the northeastern United States, nine predictors and six biogeographic
contrasts. `node_contrasts()` codes each node of the tree as a contrast between its two
clades. This tree has no branch lengths; with them, `branch_lengths = TRUE` gives the coding
of the supplement of the article.

```{r}
nodes <- node_contrasts(daphniids$tree)
dim(nodes)
```

`node_test()` regresses each contrast on the predictors. The 9999 permutations of the
article suit the false discovery rate. We use the default of 999 here to keep the page quick
to build, with nodes in parallel on two cores.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
out <- node_test(daphniids$comm, nodes, daphniids$env, daphniids$biogeography, n_perm = 999,
                 cores = 2)
out
```

The p-values answer different questions, so this choice comes first. `p_max` tests the
association between predictors and phylogeny, and it needs both permutations to reject. With
13 species, permutations of species have little power, so nothing passes it here. Permuting
sites alone tests whether a predictor matters for that contrast, whether or not that comes
from phylogeny. The figures below use sites, as this recovers most of the results of the
article, and should be read with that limit in mind.

`plot_node_test()` places the results on the tree, as in Figure 3 of the article.

```{r, fig.alt = "Phylogeny of daphniids with blue circles for predictors and red triangles for biogeographic events at the nodes, labelled with the names of the variables."}
plot_node_test(out, daphniids$tree, test = "site")
```

A tree of this size reads best as a phylogram. For very large trees, `type = "fan"` draws the
same plot in less space.

`plot_node_heatmap()` gives the direction and size of each association, as in Table S1 of
the article.

```{r, fig.alt = "Table of nodes by variables coloured by the semipartial correlation, with significant values in bold."}
plot_node_heatmap(out, test = "site")
```

A positive value means that the second clade of the node, in the order of the tree, is
favoured where the predictor is high.

## Coding biogeographic events

`biogeography_matrix()` builds the events from the area of each site. Events should come from
a hypothesis stated in advance, as the areas on the two sides of a barrier (Leibold et al.
2010; Leibold & Chase 2018). Here, three
regions are separated by two barriers, and the later one splits the last two regions.

```{r}
region <- rep(c("north", "centre", "south", NA), c(8, 6, 6, 10))
events <- list(barrier = list("north", c("centre", "south")),
               river = list("centre", "south"))
head(biogeography_matrix(region, events, min_sites = 3))
```

`contrast = "others"` compares each area with the rest, for example each refugium with the
other refugia. It needs no hypothesis about how areas relate, so it asks a weaker question.

Sites of an area are often neighbours, and free permutations then reject too often. We
simulated 1000 metacommunities on a torus of 15 by 15 sites, with communities that followed a
hidden autocorrelated environment and two blocks of 25 sites placed at random, so that events
had no effect (`data-raw/validation_events.R`). Free permutations rejected 45.1% of the tests
of a node at the 5% level, and permutations from `torus_permutations()`, given in
`site_permutations`, rejected 4.8%. The events in the figures above used free permutations,
so they should be read with this in mind.

A torus does not fit real landscapes, which have edges. `patch_permutations()` splits each
area into patches of neighbouring sites and places each patch around a site drawn at random,
which keeps the number and size of patches but not their shape or place.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
area_moves <- patch_permutations(coords, events, n_perm = 999)
node_test(comm, nodes, env, events, area_permutations = area_moves)
```

We evaluated it in a square of 20 by 20 sites, a strip of 50 by 8 and an irregular band of
436 sites, with 200 replicates of each scenario (`data-raw/validation_edges.R`). Areas were
two compact blocks, irregular areas of several patches, or one such area against all other
sites. Without effect of areas, free permutations rejected 44% to 55% of the tests of a node
at the 5% level, and `patch_permutations()` 3.0% to 6.3%. Permutations of a torus, used in the
square although it has edges, rejected 5.8% to 7.1%. When areas moved the environment of their
sites, the rejection rate of `patch_permutations()` rose to 11% to 32%. It was lowest for
compact blocks and highest for one area against the others, and the effect of an area does not
reach all nodes, so these values are not the power for a node with an effect.

The hidden environment above had a kernel bandwidth of 3 sites. With bandwidths of 6, 12 and
25 sites, up to the scale of the landscape, and no effect of areas, `patch_permutations()`
rejected 2.2% to 6.0% and free permutations 49% to 75%. It was conservative for one area
against the others (2.2% to 3.9%). The torus rejected 5.6% to 9.5% in the square.

These rates average over places of areas. Patches are placed independently, so the distance
between the two sides of an event is not kept. With areas fixed in the square, the rate was
0.4% to 2% for adjacent areas and 6% to 10% for areas in opposite corners or halves of the
landscape, and 15% to 16% with sparse sites and the default `gap`. The test is thus liberal for
sides far apart and conservative for neighbouring sides, and p-values near the threshold need
caution.

`rigid_permutations()` keeps those distances. It moves the whole event at once, by a rotation
or a reflection and a translation, as the torus-translation test of Harms et al. (2001) without
the wrap-around, so each side keeps its shape and the sides keep their distance.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
area_moves <- rigid_permutations(coords, events, n_perm = 999)
node_test(comm, nodes, env, events, area_permutations = area_moves)
```

With 150 replicates (`data-raw/validation_rigid.R`) and no effect of areas, it rejected 3.7% to
4.7% for areas placed at random in the square and the strip, 2.2% to 3.5% for adjacent and
several small areas fixed in the square, and 4.2% to 4.8% for adjacent areas, an L shape and two
areas at a short distance when the hidden environment had an exponential covariance. With sparse
sites and areas in opposite corners, it rejected less than 1%. Power for adjacent areas was
about twice that of `patch_permutations()` (24% against 13%).

The price is that an event that spans the landscape has little room to move. Two halves, two
strips along opposite edges or areas in opposite corners had one placement besides the observed
one, and most random areas in the band had none or fewer than 20. The function then returns
fewer permutations, with a warning, or stops, and `node_test()` prints how many each event got.
With fewer than 19 no node can reach the 5% level. Such an event cannot be tested by moving it
whole, by this or by any other permutation that keeps its shape.

`independent` lets parts of an event farther apart than that distance move on their own, which
gives placements to sides far apart, but assumes that the community is not spatially
autocorrelated beyond it.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
area_moves <- rigid_permutations(coords, events, n_perm = 999, independent = 10)
```

With `independent = 10`, random areas in the three landscapes gave 3.9% to 5.5%, but areas in
opposite corners gave 6% to 7% with autocorrelation over 3 or 4 sites and 12% over 12 sites, and
strips along opposite edges 8% to 9%, against 2% to 3% with `patch_permutations()`. We found no
null model that is valid for sides far apart at any range of autocorrelation, so that range has
to be argued from outside the data, and results should be compared across values.

As a guide, use `rigid_permutations()` when the sides have room to move, and compare it with
`patch_permutations()` and values of `independent` when they do not. Coordinates off a regular
lattice get random moves, and were less precise, with 2% to 9% in a square with jitter (60
replicates). There a large part of an event in an irregular region seldom fits after a move; it
then stays nearly in place while small parts move, and the function warns.

Both are methods of this package without published evaluation, tested only in these
simulations. Coordinates should be projected, and with `patch_permutations()` landscapes with
parts far apart may give patches that cross the gaps.

## How much of the phylogenetic structure is due to environment and space?

For this question we need a tree with branch lengths and sites with coordinates, so we
simulate them with the generator of Appendix C of Peres-Neto et al. (2012). In the first
scenario, two independent gradients act on species.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(32, beta = 10)
gradients <- logistic_gradients(1)
sim <- simulate_logistic(tree, gradients[c("x", "y")])
keep <- rowSums(sim$abundance) > 0
comm <- sim$abundance[keep, ]
comm <- comm[, colSums(comm) > 0]
x <- gradients$x[keep]
y <- gradients$y[keep]
```

A high `beta` gives a balanced tree, as in that appendix. `phylo_vector()` tests whether a gradient is related to the phylogeny and, if so, gives a
vector of species values for the next step. Here we ask this for each gradient.

```{r}
first <- phylo_vector(comm, tree, x, n_perm = 199)
second <- phylo_vector(comm, tree, y, n_perm = 199)
c(first$p_max, second$p_max)
```

`trait_partition()` then splits the variation of these vectors among sites. The vectors are
chosen to fit the gradients, so this step only makes sense after a significant global test.

```{r}
vectors <- cbind(first$pev_brown, second$pev_brown)
partition <- trait_partition(comm, vectors, x, y, n_perm = 199)
partition
round(partition$semipartial, 2)
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Two overlapping bars along the total variation, for environment and space, sharing the fraction b, followed by the unexplained fraction."}
plot_trait_partition(partition, labels = c("Gradient x", "Gradient y"))
```

The test of each trait against each predictor is a different question, for which ter Braak
(2019) is the reference.

Leibold, M. A., & Chase, J. M. (2018). *Metacommunity Ecology*. Monographs in Population
Biology 59. Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctt1wf4d24

Leibold, M. A., Economo, E. P., & Peres-Neto, P. (2010). Metacommunity phylogenetics:
separating the roles of environmental filters and historical biogeography. *Ecology
Letters*, 13, 1290--1299. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2010.01523.x

Peres-Neto, P. R., Leibold, M. A., & Dray, S. (2012). Assessing the effects of spatial
contingency and environmental filtering on metacommunity phylogenetics. *Ecology*, 93,
S14--S30. https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0494.1

ter Braak, C. J. F. (2019). New robust weighted averaging- and model-based methods for
assessing trait-environment relationships. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, 10,
1962--1971. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13278
